# Spec: Named Plugin Repositories

Status: draft for discussion (PR \#313)

Baseline for all compatibility statements: the **released** hcli (public GitHub index only). The current PR branch (merged API endpoint, merged-URL migration, `url-migrated` marker, `using_default_plugin_repo` hint) is unreleased and is **replaced** by this design, not migrated from.

## 1\. Concept

- A **repo** is a named URL serving a plugin-repository JSON document. Today it looks like:

```json
{
  "Version": 1,
  "Paths": {
    "ida-install-dir": "/Applications/IDA Professional 9.4.app"
  },
  "Settings": {
    "plugin-repository": {
      "url": "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HexRaysSA/plugin-repository/refs/heads/v1/plugin-repository.json"
    }
  },
  "Plugins": {...}
  }
}

```

- `ida-config.json` holds a map of named repos plus one **default** repo.  
- hcli fetches repos independently (lazily) and merges client-side, so provenance is always known. No server-side merging.  
- No reserved names. The two shipped defaults:

| Name | URL | Auth |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| `community` | `https://community.plugins.hex-rays.com/plugin-repository.json` | anonymous |
| `hexrays` | `https://hexrays.plugins.hex-rays.com/plugin-repository.json` | required (401 otherwise) |

- Our repository are on \*.plugins.hex-rays.com  
- Credentials are attached per existing host scoping (\*.plugins.hex-rays.com only) — unchanged.  
- **Plugin identity stays `name@host`** (`urls.repository`). A repo is where a plugin was *found*, never part of what it *is*.

## 2\. Reference grammar

```
plugin-ref := [repo "/"] name [version-spec]
            | name [version-spec] "@" host-url        (existing, unchanged)
            | https-url | file-url                    (existing, unchanged)
```

- The `repo/` prefix is **lookup scope only**: it selects which document to search, is dropped after resolution, and is never stored. Validated as `^[a-z0-9\-]+$`.  
- The grammar is already unambiguous: plugin names are validated as `^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+$`, so `/` cannot appear in a name. No schema change.  
- Version specs compose: `hexrays/xyz@url>=1.2`.

## 3\. Resolution

| Input | Search space | Fetches |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| `xyz` | default repos only | default repo doc |
| `hexrays/xyz community/xyz` | repo `hexrays` only repo `community` only | that repo doc |
| `xyz@<url>` | all configured repos (host disambiguates) | as needed |

- Miss in the searched scope → plain "plugin not found". No cross-repo suggestions; no repo is special.  
- `hexrays/xyz` while logged out → the repo fetch gets a 401 → `PluginAccessDeniedError` → clear "log in to access repo 'hexrays'" message (mechanism already exists in `fetch_plugin_repo_bytes`).  
- Collisions within one repo: unchanged — `AmbiguousPluginReferenceError` listing `name@url` candidates.  
- Install flows: `install xyz` for community plugins works exactly as released; private plugins are always `install hexrays/xyz`, so once installed there is no ambiguity.

## 4\. Changes required

### Server (outside this repo)

- S1: serve the two documents above; `hexrays` returns 401 anonymous and only entitled entries when authenticated. Drop the merged endpoint.  
- S2: portal enforces unique plugin names within the `hexrays` document.  
- S3 (exists): portal is sole issuer of \*.`plugins.hex-rays.com` identities; community indexer keeps `expected_host` enforcement.

### Config — `src/hcli/lib/ida/__init__.py`

- Replace `PluginRepositoryConfig` (single `url`) with a named map \+ defaults:

```json
{
  "Version": 1,
  "Paths": {
    "ida-install-dir": "/Applications/IDA Professional 9.4.app"
  },
  "Settings": {
    "plugin-repositories": { 
      "hexrays": {
        "url": "https://hexrays.plugins.hex-rays.com/plugin-repository.json",
      },
      "community": {
        "url": "https://community.plugins.hex-rays.com/plugin-repository.json"
      }
    },
    "default-plugin-repositories": ["hexrays", "community"],
  },
  "Plugins": {...}
  }
}

```

- Replace `get_plugin_repository_url()` / `get_default_plugin_repository_url()` with map-aware equivalents; default URLs derive from `ENV.HCLI_API_URL`.  
- Remove the branch's merged-URL migration and `url-migrated` marker.

### Reference parsing — `src/hcli/lib/ida/plugin/reference.py`

- `PluginReference` gains `repo: str | None`; `parse_plugin_reference` peels a leading `repo/`. Whether `repo/name@host` is allowed (scope \+ identity) or an error: open question OQ1.

### Repo layer — `src/hcli/lib/ida/plugin/repo/`

- New aggregate over `{name: BasePluginRepo}` \+ default name, lazy per-repo fetch, implementing the resolution table above. Fits under the existing `BasePluginRepo` abstraction.

### Command wiring — `src/hcli/commands/plugin/`

- Group callback builds the aggregate from config. `--repo <url>` unchanged in meaning: an ephemeral repo used as the sole/default scope (repo prefixes rejected under it).  
- Naming conflict: `--repo github` currently means "run the live GitHub indexer". Resolve by renaming that magic value (OQ2). Shipped repo names `community`/`hexrays` avoid the collision.  
- `install`/`upgrade`/`bundle`: thread `ref.repo` into lookups. `upgrade` stays anchored to the installed `name@host` and resolves it across configured repos; an explicit repo prefix acts as scope, mismatch mirrors the existing `@url` mismatch error.  
- `search`: aggregates all fetchable repos (skips repos it cannot fetch, e.g. 401 while logged out); results show provenance as `repo/name` for non-default repos; JSON output gains an additive `repo` field. Repos that could not be access (either because of 401 or 404\) are mentionned in the end of the search \- Error should be specific to error code   
- Remove the branch's `using_default_plugin_repo` login-hint plumbing (superseded by the 401 path).

### Repo management commands

- `hcli plugin repo list | add <name> <url> | remove <name> | set-default <name>` editing the config map. Shipped entries are ordinary entries: renamable, removable, default reassignable.

## 5\. Compatibility (vs released hcli)

- `install <name>` for community plugins: identical behavior. Default repo serves the same index content, now via the API URL.  
- `name@url` references: unchanged.  
- `--repo <url>`, bundle, fs, file/https direct installs, offline: unchanged.  
- Installed plugins: records already store `name@host` and only private repos can have \*.plugins.hex-rays.com hosts; `upgrade`/`status` resolve identically. No installed-state change.  
- JSON outputs: additive fields only.  
- New capability, no regression: private plugins via `hexrays/<name>`.

## 6\. Migration (from released state only)

- M1: `ida-config.json` with the legacy raw.githubusercontent URL as `plugin-repository.url` (the released default) or no entry → write the new two-repo map with `community` as default.  
- M2: a user-customized `plugin-repository.url` → becomes a named entry (e.g. `custom`) and the default repo; behavior preserved.  
- M3: one-shot rewrite, no marker needed — the old single-`url` key is removed by the rewrite, so it cannot re-trigger. Console notice on migration, as already agreed.  
- M4: portal/docs publish the canonical `hcli plugin install hexrays/<name>` string.

## 7\. Out of scope (v1)

- Provenance in installed records (which repo installed a plugin): not needed with identity-based resolution; revisit only if user-defined repos with overlapping identities become common.  
- Repo priorities/overlays: deliberately excluded — scope is always explicit or the single default.

## 8\. Open questions

- OQ1: `repo/name@host` — allow as scope restriction, or reject : Answer: ALLOW   
- OQ2: new name for the `--repo github` indexer mode: This should go in a specific hcli plugin index command (make a suggestion for this)   
- OQ3: config JSON shape final form (naming, casing) — align with IDA's conventions for `ida-config.json`.  
- OQ4: should `search` while logged out mention that a configured repo was skipped for auth (one grey line), or stay silent? \=\> it should mention it as a message after search
I'll survey the PR changes and the existing documentation in parallel.

Named plugin repositories, with authenticated access to private plugins
Replaces the single `plugin-repository` URL with named repositories, so hcli can install private, entitlement-gated plugins alongside public ones and always knows which repository served what.

## Configuration

`.Settings.plugin-repositories` is a map of name → url, plus `.Settings.default-plugin-repository`. Two entries are reserved — `community` and `hexrays` — always present, always their Hex-Rays URLs. A config that tries to repoint one is ignored on that point and told so: a reserved name whose URL can be changed is worth nothing, and `hexrays` is exactly the name an attacker would want, because it is the name credentials follow.

Managed with `hcli plugin repo list | add | remove | set-default`.

## Scope depends on the operation

Searching is a survey; installing is a choice.

| operation | searches | on 401 |
|---|---|---|
| `search` | every configured repository | skip, and report it |
| `install xyz` | the default repository only | never happens — no credentials sent |
| `install hexrays/xyz` | that repository alone | fatal |
| `upgrade` | all repositories, anchored by installed host | skip |

A bare `install` never touches an authenticated repository, so a logged-out user never sees a 401 for a plugin they weren't asking for. A `repo/` prefix is an explicit request, so failing it is the honest answer.

Repositories are never overlaid, so cross-repository name collisions do not arise: a bare name resolves in the default repository only, exactly as released hcli resolves it against its single repository, and a private plugin is always named explicitly. Collisions *within* one repository behave as before.

## Credentials

`fetch_plugin_repo_bytes` walks redirects by hand rather than letting httpx follow them. httpx strips `Authorization` across origins but forwards `x-api-key` — which would hand a credential to whatever host a repository 302s to. Each hop re-decides; the logged-in state resolves once per fetch because it can cost a network round-trip.

`is_plugin_repo_host` is the only predicate for where those credentials go: HTTPS on `plugins.hex-rays.com` or a subdomain. Deliberately separate from the API client's `ENV.HCLI_API_URL` scoping — the two answer different questions, and widening one must not widen the other.

## Identity spoofing

The aggregate drops any plugin claiming a `plugins.hex-rays.com` identity from a repository other than `hexrays`. Adding a repository must not confer the power to impersonate us: `upgrade` resolves an installed plugin by host across every configured repository, so without this, a repository the user added could take over upgrades of a genuinely installed private plugin.

## Migration

One-shot, no marker — it removes the key it reads. A customized URL survives as a repository named `custom` that becomes the default, which is what preserves that user's unprefixed installs; it is far more likely to be a repository of their own than a mirror of ours.

Also adds `extra="allow"` across the `ida-config.json` models. Without it every write silently dropped keys IDA owns but hcli doesn't model — a pre-existing bug, and a precondition for a migration that rewrites the file.

## Compatibility

Public flow is unchanged: search, install, upgrade and status for a GitHub-hosted plugin behave exactly as released. `--repo`, bundles, and offline installs are untouched. JSON output gains fields only.

## Verification

Against the live repositories: `community` fetches anonymously (127 plugins), `hexrays` 401s anonymously and returns 3 plugins with an API key, and a private archive downloads with a matching sha256. Install, status and upgrade complete for a private plugin. A local-server test confirms the credential is attached on an eligible hop and dropped across a cross-origin redirect.

## Server dependency

Requires the `hexrays` and `community` documents (already live). The three private plugins have been updated to three-segment identities; hcli accepts two- and three-segment forms so already-installed plugins keep working through the transition.

86	### Disambiguating plugin names
87	
88	When two plugins share the same bare name in the repository (for example, different forks of the same project), HCLI cannot tell which one you mean from the name alone. 93	Choose one of:

96	```

103	```

1	# IDA Plugin Repository Architecture
2	
3	## Core Components
4	
5	1. **User-facing portal showcasing the plugins** - The [plugins.hex-rays.com](https://plugins.hex-rays.com/) is a web interface to the collection of available IDA Pro plugins.
6	2. **JSON Index** - The new plugin repository publishes a JSON document within [github.com/HexRaysSA/plugin-repository](https://github.com/HexRaysSA/plugin-repository). This file is the index of all available plugins, their versions and metadata, and download URLs.
7	3. **GitHub Actions** - GitHub Actions runs regularly to update the JSON document with plugins discovered across GitHub. The raw index data is available [here](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HexRaysSA/plugin-repository/refs/heads/v1/plugin-repository.json).
8	4. **Named repositories** - hcli reads its repositories from `.Settings.plugin-repositories` in `ida-config.json` and merges them client-side, so it always knows which repository served a plugin. Two are shipped and reserved: `community` (`https://community.plugins.hex-rays.com/plugin-repository.json`, anonymous) and `hexrays` (`https://hexrays.plugins.hex-rays.com/plugin-repository.json`, which requires `hcli login` and serves only the private plugins your account is entitled to). Manage the rest with `hcli plugin repo list | add | remove | set-default`.
9	
10	    A reference may name a repository: `hcli plugin install hexrays/<name>`. Without a prefix it resolves in the repository named by `.Settings.default-plugin-repository` (`community` by default), while `hcli plugin search` spans every configured repository and reports any it could not reach.
11	
12	
13	## How It Works
14	
15	The plugin repository's GitHub Action watches for GitHub repositories that contain an `ida-plugin.json` file.
16	For each repo, it will watch for releases. When it sees a release, it will inspect the release archives for either source archives (pure-Python) or binary archives (containing .so/.dll/.dylib plugins).
17	In either case, it'll expect to find an `ida-plugin.json` file in the archive describing the plugin.
18	The service will index all the found archives and their metadata, and expose this to HCLI
19	(and/or other plugin managers, like a planned GUI version within IDA).
20	
21	!!! note
22	
23	    The plugin repository requires additional metadata compared to the initial version documented on the Hex-Rays docs website.
24	
25	
26	## IDA Plugin Manager
27	
28	HCLI uses the plugin repository JSON file to list/search for plugins and retrieve the download URL.
29	After various validation steps, HCLI then extracts the archive subdirectory containing
30	 `ida-plugin.json` into `$IDAUSR/plugins/`, and the plugin is installed.
31	If there are Python dependencies declared within the metadata file, then these are installed via pip first.
32	There are obvious upgrade and uninstallation routines, too.
33	
34	### Plugin Installation Location
35	
36	Plugins are installed to `$IDAUSR/plugins/`, where `$IDAUSR` is the IDA user directory: 
37	
38	- **Windows**: `%APPDATA%\Hex-Rays\IDA Pro\`
39	- **macOS**: `~/Library/Application Support/IDA Pro/`
40	- **Linux**: `~/.idapro/`
41	
42	It's possible to override `$IDAUSR` when running IDA, which can be helpful if you test across multiple versions:
43	
44	```
45	$ export IDAUSR=~/.idapro91/
46	$ hcli plugin install ipyida
47	$ ~/software/ida-9.1/ida
48	```
49	
50	Each plugin is installed in its own subdirectory within `plugins/`. For example, installing the "oplog" plugin creates:
51	```
52	$IDAUSR/plugins/oplog/
53	├── ida-plugin.json
54	├── oplog_entry.py
55	└── (other plugin files)
56	```
57	
58	The directory name matches the plugin name from `ida-plugin.json`.
59	This is why the contents of `name` are fairly restrictive. They should also be globally unique.
60	
61	During upgrades, the existing directory is replaced with the new version.
62	Uninstallation is as easy as deleting the directory.
63	
64	### Plugin identity and name collisions
65	
66	In the repository index, a plugin is identified by the pair `(name, repository URL)`. Two plugins with the same bare name from different repositories are distinct entries, and the repository URL is normalized (lowercased scheme/host/path, trailing slash stripped) before comparison so that cosmetic URL differences do not split a single plugin into two.
67	
68	On disk, however, plugins still install as `$IDAUSR/plugins/<name>`. Name is therefore the installed-layout identity, and only one plugin with a given bare name can be installed at a time. When the repository contains multiple plugins with the same name, HCLI requires a qualified reference of the form `name@repository-url` (optionally with a version spec, e.g. `name==1.2.3@repository-url`). An installed plugin's local metadata records its source repository, so status and upgrade operations anchor their repository lookups on the installed plugin's host and stay consistent even when the bare name is ambiguous in the repository.
69

1	# How to Test Your Plugin Before Publishing
2	
3	This guide shows you how to thoroughly test your IDA plugin before publishing it to the plugin repository, ensuring it meets quality standards and works correctly across different environments.
4	
5	## Problem Statement
6	
7	You've developed an IDA plugin and want to test it comprehensively before releasing it to ensure:
8	
9	- The plugin metadata is valid
10	- It installs correctly
11	- It works across supported IDA versions
12	- Python dependencies are properly declared
13	- There are no common packaging errors
14	
15	## Prerequisites
16	
17	- HCLI installed (see [Installation](../getting-started/installation.md))
18	- Your plugin with `ida-plugin.json` file
19	- Valid IDA Pro installation (for runtime testing)
20	- Authentication configured (for dependency installation)
21	
22	## Quick Validation Checklist
23	
24	Before deep testing, ensure these basics:
25	
26	- [ ] `ida-plugin.json` exists in plugin root
27	- [ ] Plugin version follows semantic versioning (e.g., `1.0.0`)
28	- [ ] Repository URL is correct
29	- [ ] Entry point file exists
30	- [ ] No trailing commas in JSON
31	
32	## Step-by-Step Testing Guide
33	
34	### Step 1: Validate Plugin Metadata with Lint
35	
36	The first step is to validate your plugin structure and metadata:
37	
38	```bash
39	hcli plugin lint /path/to/your-plugin
40	```
41	
42	**For a directory:**
43	
44	```bash
45	cd /path/to/your-plugin
46	hcli plugin lint .
47	```
48	
49	**For a ZIP archive:**
50	
51	```bash
52	hcli plugin lint your-plugin-v1.0.0.zip
53	```
54	
55	**For a GitHub release:**
56	
57	```bash
58	hcli plugin lint https://github.com/username/plugin/releases/download/v1.0.0/plugin.zip
59	```
60	
61	### Step 2: Understand Lint Output
62	
63	**Success output:**
64	
65	```
66	✓ Plugin validation successful!
67	
68	Plugin: my-awesome-plugin
69	Version: 1.0.0
70	Entry Point: plugin_entry.py
71	IDA Versions: 9.1, 9.2
72	Platforms: windows-x86_64, linux-x86_64, macos-aarch64
73	
74	Warnings:
75	  - Consider adding keywords to improve discoverability
76	  - No description provided
77	
78	Suggestions:
79	  - Add a logo (logoPath) for better visibility in the plugin browser
80	```
81	
82	**Error output:**
83	
84	```
85	✗ Plugin validation failed!
86	
87	Errors:
88	  - Missing required field: plugin.version
89	  - Invalid JSON: Unexpected token '}' at line 15
90	  - Entry point file 'plugin.py' not found
91	  - Python dependency 'requets' not found on PyPI (did you mean 'requests'?)
92	
93	Fix these errors before publishing.
94	```
95	
96	### Step 3: Fix Common Validation Errors
97	
98	#### Error: "Invalid JSON syntax"
99	
100	**Cause:** Trailing commas or syntax errors in `ida-plugin.json`.
101	
102	**Solution:** Use a JSON validator or `jq`:
103	
104	```bash
105	cat ida-plugin.json | jq .
106	```
107	
108	Fix trailing commas:
109	
110	```json
111	{
112	  "plugin": {
113	    "name": "my-plugin",
114	    "version": "1.0.0"  // ← Remove comma if this is the last field
115	  }
116	}
117	```
118	
119	#### Error: "Missing required field: plugin.version"
120	
121	**Cause:** Version field is missing or empty.
122	
123	**Solution:** Add semantic version:
124	
125	```json
126	{
127	  "plugin": {
128	    "version": "1.0.0"
129	  }
130	}
131	```
132	
133	#### Error: "Entry point file not found"
134	
135	**Cause:** File specified in `entryPoint` doesn't exist.
136	
137	**Solution:** Verify the file exists and path is correct. This path is relative to `ida-plugin.json`:
138	
139	```bash
140	# Check entry point
141	ls -l plugin_entry.py
142	
143	# Update ida-plugin.json
144	{
145	  "plugin": {
146	    "entryPoint": "plugin_entry.py"  // Must match actual filename
147	  }
148	}
149	```
150	
151	#### Error: "Python dependency not found on PyPI"
152	
153	**Cause:** Typo in dependency name or package doesn't exist.
154	
155	**Solution:** Verify package exists:
156	
157	```bash
158	pip search requests  # or check pypi.org
159	```
160	
161	Fix in `ida-plugin.json`:
162	
163	```json
164	{
165	  "plugin": {
166	    "pythonDependencies": [
167	      "requests>=2.28.0",  // ← Fixed typo from "requets"
168	      "pydantic>=2.0"
169	    ]
170	  }
171	}
172	```
173	
174	#### Error: "Invalid version specifier"
175	
176	**Cause:** Version doesn't follow semantic versioning.
177	
178	**Solution:** Use format `MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH`:
179	
180	```json
181	// ✗ Wrong
182	{"version": "1.0"}
183	{"version": "v1.0.0"}
184	{"version": "1.01.0"}
185	{"version": "1.0.0-beta"}  // Pre-release tags not fully supported yet
186	
187	// ✓ Correct
188	{"version": "1.0.0"}
189	{"version": "2.1.3"}
190	```
191	
192	### Step 4: Test Local Installation
193	
194	Install your plugin from the local directory:
195	
196	```bash
197	# Install from directory
198	hcli plugin install /path/to/your-plugin
199	
200	# Or from ZIP
201	hcli plugin install ./your-plugin-v1.0.0.zip
202	```
203	
204	Expected output:
205	
206	```
207	Installing plugin: my-awesome-plugin==1.0.0
208	Installing Python dependencies: requests>=2.28.0, pydantic>=2.0
209	✓ Installed plugin: my-awesome-plugin==1.0.0
210	```
211	
212	### Step 5: Verify Installation
213	
214	Check that the plugin is installed:
215	
216	```bash
217	hcli plugin status
218	```
219	
220	Output should include your plugin:
221	
222	```
223	✓ my-awesome-plugin    1.0.0    /path/to/.idapro/plugins/my-awesome-plugin/
224	  requests             2.31.0
225	  pydantic             2.5.0
226	```
227	
228	Verify plugin files were copied:
229	
230	```bash

233	
234	# Windows
235	dir %APPDATA%\.idapro\plugins\my-awesome-plugin\
236	```
237	
238	### Step 6: Test in IDA Pro
239	
240	Launch IDA Pro and verify:
241	
242	1. **Plugin loads without errors:**
243	   - Check IDA console output for Python errors
244	   - Look for your plugin in Edit → Plugins menu
245	
246	2. **Plugin functionality works:**
247	   - Execute main plugin features
248	   - Test edge cases
249	   - Verify hotkeys (if any)
250	
251	3. **Check for errors:**
252	   ```python
253	   # In IDA Python console
254	   import ida_loader
255	
256	   ida_loader.load_and_run_plugin("my-awesome-plugin", 0)
257	   ```
258	
259	### Step 7: Test Across IDA Versions
260	
261	If your plugin supports multiple IDA versions, test each one:
262	
263	```bash
264	# Set specific IDA installation
265	export HCLI_CURRENT_IDA_INSTALL_DIR="/Applications/IDA Professional 9.1.app"
266	hcli plugin install /path/to/your-plugin
267	
268	# Test in IDA 9.1
269	/Applications/IDA\ Professional\ 9.1.app/Contents/MacOS/ida64
270

272	export HCLI_CURRENT_IDA_INSTALL_DIR="/Applications/IDA Professional 9.2.app"
273	hcli plugin install /path/to/your-plugin --force
274	
275	# Test in IDA 9.2
276	/Applications/IDA\ Professional\ 9.2.app/Contents/MacOS/ida64
277	```
278	
279	**Verify:**
280	
281	- No API compatibility issues
282	- All features work as expected
283	- No deprecation warnings
284	
285	### Step 8: Test Plugin Configuration (if applicable)
286	
287	If your plugin uses settings:
288	
289	```bash
290	# List plugin settings
291	hcli plugin config list my-awesome-plugin
292	
293	# Set a configuration value
294	hcli plugin config set my-awesome-plugin api_key "test-key-123"
295	
296	# Get the value

299	# Test in plugin

301	```
302	
303	### Step 9: Test Uninstallation
304	
305	Verify clean removal:
306	
307	```bash
308	hcli plugin uninstall my-awesome-plugin
309	```
310	
311	Check that files are removed:
312	
313	```bash
314	ls ~/.idapro/plugins/my-awesome-plugin/  # Should not exist
315	```
316	
317	Re-install to continue testing:
318	
319	```bash
320	hcli plugin install /path/to/your-plugin
321	```
322	
323	## Pre-Publishing Checklist
324	
325	Before creating a GitHub release:
326	
327	### Metadata Completeness
328	
329	- [ ] `version` follows semantic versioning
330	- [ ] `description` is clear and concise
331	- [ ] `keywords` added for discoverability
332	- [ ] `license` specified
333	- [ ] `authors` and/or `maintainers` with email
334	- [ ] `urls.repository` points to correct GitHub repo
335	- [ ] `idaVersions` lists all supported versions
336	- [ ] `platforms` specified (or omit for all platforms)
337	- [ ] `logoPath` included (optional but recommended)
338	
339	### Testing Complete
340	
341	- [ ] `hcli plugin lint` passes without errors
342	- [ ] Plugin installs from ZIP archive
343	- [ ] Plugin loads in IDA Pro without errors
344	- [ ] Core functionality works as expected
345	- [ ] Tested on all supported IDA versions
346	- [ ] Python dependencies install correctly
347	- [ ] Settings/configuration works (if applicable)
348	- [ ] Plugin uninstalls cleanly
349	
350	### Documentation
351	
352	- [ ] README.md with usage instructions
353	- [ ] CHANGELOG.md with version history
354	- [ ] LICENSE file included
355	- [ ] Example usage provided
356	- [ ] Known issues documented
357	
358	### Repository Setup
359	
360	- [ ] GitHub repository is public
361	- [ ] `ida-plugin.json` is present
362	- [ ] Release tags follow semantic versioning (e.g., `v1.0.0`)
363	- [ ] ZIP archive attached to release (for non-Python plugins)
364	- [ ] Release notes describe changes
365	
366	
367	## Common Testing Pitfalls
368	
369	### 1. Not Testing on Clean IDA Installation
370	
371	**Problem:** Plugin works on your system but fails for users.
372	
373	**Solution:** Test with fresh IDA installation:
374	
375	```bash
376	# Backup existing plugins
377	mv ~/.idapro/plugins ~/.idapro/plugins.bak
378	
379	# Test plugin installation
380	hcli plugin install /path/to/plugin
381	
382	# Restore
383	mv ~/.idapro/plugins.bak ~/.idapro/plugins
384	```
385	
386	### 2. Hardcoded Paths
387	
388	**Problem:** Plugin uses absolute paths that don't exist on other systems.
389	
390	**Solution:** Use IDA SDK functions:
391	
392	```python
393	import ida_diskio
394	import idaapi
395	
396	# ✗ Wrong
397	config_path = "/Users/me/.plugin-config"
398	
399	# ✓ Correct
400	config_path = os.path.join(ida_diskio.get_user_idadir(), "plugin-config")
401	```
402	
403	### 3. Missing Python Dependency Versions
404	
405	**Problem:** Plugin works with latest dependency but breaks with older versions.
406	
407	**Solution:** Specify minimum versions:
408	
409	```json
410	{
411	  "pythonDependencies": [
412	    "requests>=2.28.0",  // Specify minimum version
413	    "pydantic>=2.0,<3.0" // Or version range
414	  ]
415	}
416	```
417	
418	Prefer not to pin to specific versions (`==2.28.0`) because it's difficult for many plugins to agree on precisely the same version.

3	## Why Publish Your Plugin?

5	As the author of an existing or new plugin, we encourage you to make the following updates so that your project is compatible with the HCLI and Plugin Manager, and can benefit from the new ecosystem. 
6	
7	Making your plugin available via Plugin Manager offers several benefits:
8	
9	  - simplified plugin installation
10	  - improved plugin discoverability through the central index
11	  - easy Python dependency management
12	
13	
14	If you have any questions, open an issue on [this repo](https://github.com/HexRaysSA/ida-hcli) or contact our [support](https://support.hex-rays.com/).
15	
16

18

24	## Steps to Publication
25	
26	The key points to make your IDA plugin available via Plugin Manager are:
27	
28	  1. Update `ida-plugin.json`
29	  2. Package your plugin into a ZIP archive
30	  3. Publish releases on GitHub
31	
32	For further details on how your plugin fits into the greater ecosystem, you can also review:
33	
34	  - [Plugin packaging and format](./plugin-packaging-and-format.md)
35	  - [Plugin repository architecture](./plugin-repository-architecture.md)
36	
37	
38	The plugin ecosystem is fully automated. After you publish a new GitHub release with updated metadata, your plugin will automatically be indexed and made available to IDA users.
39	
40	
41	### 1. Update or create `ida-plugin.json`
42	
43	IDA 9.0 introduced `ida-plugin.json` as a way to [declare metadata about plugins](https://docs.hex-rays.com/developer/publishing-plugins/how-tos/plugin-publishing), such as name and entry point.
44	We extend this format with **new required and optional fields** to ensure compatibility with HCLI and the Plugin Manager, and to make the metadata more informative.
45	
46	A minimal `ida-plugin.json` file now looks like:
47	
48	```json
49	{
50	  "$schema": "https://hcli.docs.hex-rays.com/schemas/ida-plugin.json",
51	  "IDAMetadataDescriptorVersion": 1,
52	  "plugin": {
53	    "name": "plugin1",
54	    "version": "1.0.0",
55	    "entryPoint": "plugin1.py",
56	    "urls": {
57	      "repository": "https://github.com/HexRaysSA/ida-hcli"
58	    },
59	    "authors": [{
60	      "name": "Willi Ballenthin",
61	      "email": "wballenthin@hex-rays.com"
62	    }]
63	  }
64	}
65	```
66	
67	and a more complete `ida-plugin.json` looks like:
68	
69	```json
70	{
71	  "$schema": "https://hcli.docs.hex-rays.com/schemas/ida-plugin.json",
72	  "IDAMetadataDescriptorVersion": 1,
73	  "plugin": {
74	    "name": "ida-terminal-plugin",
75	    "entryPoint": "index.py",
76	    "version": "1.0.0",
77	    "idaVersions": [
78	      "9.0",
79	      "9.1",
80	      "9.2"
81	    ],
82	    "platforms": [
83	      "windows-x86_64",
84	      "linux-x86_64",
85	      "macos-x86_64",
86	      "macos-aarch64",
87	    ],
88	    "description": "A lightweight terminal integration for IDA Pro that lets you open a fully functional terminal within the IDA GUI.\nQuickly access shell commands, scripts, or tooling without leaving your reversing environment.",
89	    "license": "MIT",
90	    "logoPath": "ida-plugin.png",
91	    "categories": [
92	      "ui-ux-and-visualization"
93	    ],
94	    "keywords": [
95	      "terminal",
96	      "shell",
97	      "cli",
98	    ],
99	    "pythonDependencies": [
100	      "pydantic>=2.12"
101	    ],
102	    "urls": {
103	      "repository": "https://github.com/williballenthin/idawilli"
104	    },
105	    "authors": [{
106	      "name": "Pierre-Alexandre Losson",
107	      "email": "palosson@hex-rays.com"
108	    }],

127	Here are the **new required** fields:
128	
129	  - `.plugin.version` is now required
130	  - `.plugin.urls.repository` is required
131	  - `.plugin.authors` and/or `.plugin.maintainers` must be provided, `.email` is required
132	
133	and new optional fields:
134	
135	  - `.plugin.pythonDependencies` is a list of packages on PyPI that will be installed
136	  - `.plugin.keywords` is a list of terms to help users searching for plugins
137	  - `.plugin.platforms` is recommended, defaults to all platforms. The possible values are: `windows-x86_64`, `linux-x86_64`, `macos-x86_64`, and `macos-aarch64`.
138	  - `.plugin.license` for the code license of your project
139	  - `.plugin.settings` is a list of descriptors of settings

143	
144	    If there's a problem with the `ida-plugin.json` file, then it will not be indexed by the plugin repository. Unfortunately even things like trailing commas will break strict JSON parsers like the one used by HCLI.  
145	    We recommend to use `hcli plugin lint /path/to/plugin[.zip]` to check for problems and suggestions.

148	### 2. Package your plugin
149	
150	You must distribute plugins via ZIP archives.
151	See [Plugin packaging and format](./plugin-packaging-and-format.md) for more details on the contents of the ZIP archives.
152	Essentially, collect the plugin files (Python source or `.dll`/`.so`/`.dylib` shared objects) and the `ida-plugin.json` and any other supporting resources into a single file.
153	
154	- For **pure-Python plugins**, you can probably rely on the source archive automatically attached to GitHub Releases and Tags.
155	- For **native plugins**, you should consider using GitHub Actions to build the artifacts - and Hex-Rays is happy to provide templates and/or propose an initial workflow. You can see an example here: [milankovo/zydisinfo .../build.yml](https://github.com/milankovo/zydisinfo/blob/main/.github/workflows/build.yml)
156	
157	#### Packaging Pure Python Plugins
158	
159	For simple single-file plugins, all you need to do is add an `ida-plugin.json` file.
160	Then do releases via GitHub Actions and the automatically attached source archive will be the plugin archive.
161	
162	In fact, most pure Python plugins can get away with no build step, and just tagging releases via GitHub Releases.
163	
164	If there are multiple plugins in the same repo, this is ok, as long as they're in separate directories.
165	See "Multi-Plugin Archives" in [Plugin packaging and format](./plugin-packaging-and-format.md).
166	
167	If a Python plugin relies on a third-party dependency, declare this in the `pythonDependencies` array in `ida-plugin.json`.
168	
169	If there's many files related to the plugin, ensure they're all in the same directory (or nested subdirectory) as `ida-plugin.json`.
170	Python plugins can rely on imports relative to the entry point script, so the following are ok:
171	
172	```
173	plugins.zip
174	└── plugin1
175	    ├── ida-plugin.json
176	    ├── plugin_entry.py
177	    └── myutils.py
178	
179	# import myutils
180	```
181	
182	or
183	
184	```
185	plugins.zip
186	└── plugin1
187	    ├── ida-plugin.json
188	    ├── plugin_entry.py
189	    └── mylib
190	        ├── __init__.py
191	        └── foo
192	
193	# import mylib.foo
194	```
195	
196	Some plugins have published most of their code to PyPI via a traditional Python package, and then refer to this in a trivial entrypoint stub.
197	This is fine. IPyIDA is an example.
198	They can keep doing this, updating `pythonDependencies` to reference that package; or they can package the Python code as a relative import.
199	
200	
201	#### Packaging a Native Plugin
202	
203	If its a native plugin, adapt the build configuration (if it exists) to GitHub Actions.
204	To acquire the SDK, either use a Git submodule or use HCLI to fetch it.
205	The latter is probably a better solution but requires an active IDA Pro license (but you can get one through the [Plugin Contributor Program](https://hex-rays.com/contributor-program)),
206	and enables you to build against 8.4, 9.0, 9.1, as well as 9.2+.
207	The open source SDK on GitHub only has tags for 9.2+.
208	
209	Here's an example workflow: [PR#4](https://github.com/milankovo/zydisinfo/pull/4)
210	
211	Once you have built the shared object files, package them up along with the `ida-plugin.json` file.
212	You can create one artifact per platform, or do a "fat" binary archive (see above).
213	Separate files might be easier; just make sure you set `.plugin.platforms` in `ida-plugin.json` to reflect the contents, so we don't try to install .dll files on macOS.
214	
215	#### Example: Packaging eset/DelphiHelper
216	
217	Because this is a pure-Python plugin, packaging was very easy! Just add the metadata file and do releases on GitHub:
218	
219	1. added `ida-plugin.json`: [PR#5](https://github.com/eset/DelphiHelper/pull/5/files)
220	2. asked to start using GitHub Releases via the web interface
221	3. ...done
222	
223	
224	#### Example: Packaging milankovo/zydishelper
225	
226	Because this is a plugin written in C++ and compiled to a native shared object, packaging took a little more work:
227	
228	1. added `ida-plugin.json`: [PR#4](https://github.com/milankovo/zydisinfo/pull/4/files#diff-601834cd7516c6a40f96dda33295f21abd1f8e96f85095ab0823375f6479da3f)
229	2. added a [workflow for GitHub Actions](https://github.com/milankovo/zydisinfo/pull/4/files#diff-5c3fa597431eda03ac3339ae6bf7f05e1a50d6fc7333679ec38e21b337cb6721) to build the plugin
230	  a. use [HCLI](https://hcli.docs.hex-rays.com/) to fetch IDA Pro SDKs for 9.0, 9.1, and 9.2
231	  b. use [ida-cmake](https://github.com/allthingsida/ida-cmake) for configuration
232	  c. matrixed across Windows/Linux/macOS runners
233	  d. build the plugin
234	  e. upload to the GitHub Releases page
235	3. asked to start using [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/milankovo/zydisinfo/releases) via the web interface
236	
237	While it took a little while to get working, this workflow should serve as a solid template for many plugins written in C++.
238	For example, we used it to kickstart the [build of the BinDiff plugin](https://github.com/HexRays-plugin-contributions/bindiff/blob/ci-gha/.github/workflows/build.yml).
239	
240	### 3. Publish releases on GitHub
241	
242	In the near term, you must use GitHub Releases to tag releases, because the plugin repository backend (initially) uses GitHub to discover and index available plugins.
243	You'll need to upload the plugin archives as attachments to the release (unless the default source archive is sufficient, which is usually true for pure-Python plugins).
244	
245	Each day, an indexer looks for GitHub repositories that contain `ida-plugin.json` and inspects the releases for candidate plugins.
246	So once you've updated the metadata file and made a new release in GitHub, your plugin will soon show up automatically!
247	
248	In other words, inclusion into the plugin repository is completely self-service - it's just a matter of putting a well-formed plugin in a place we can find it.
249	
250	!!! tip "Test your plugin"
251	
252	      Check out [our guide](../how-to/test-plugin-before-publishing.md) to test your plugin before publishing it to the new Plugin Manager ecosystem.

255	## FAQ
256	
257	### Do I need to submit my plugin anywhere?
258	
259	No, if you're using GitHub Releases to share plugin ZIP archives with valid `ida-plugin.json` files, then your plugins should be auto-included into the Hex-Rays plugin repository!
260	While there used to be an explicit submission process via My Hex-Rays portal, we've moved to a self-service flow that's (hopefully) open and transparent.
261	
262	In the future, we may re-open a web form or accept PRs to add plugins not hosted on GitHub, but this isn't supported quite yet.
263	
264	### What do I do if my plugin doesn't show up in the repo?
265	
266	1. Ensure the plugin file (the ZIP archive) is well formed: `hcli plugin lint /path/to/plugin.zip`
267	2. Check that plugin is recognized by the indexer by inspecting [plugin-repository.json](https://github.com/HexRaysSA/plugin-repository/blob/v1/plugin-repository.json).
268	    1. ensure you can find your plugin in the [search results](https://github.com/search?q=path%3A**%2Fida-plugin.json&type=code)
269	    2. otherwise, you can propose to add your plugin to the explicit list here: [known-repositories.json](https://github.com/HexRaysSA/plugin-repository/blob/v1/known-repositories.txt)
270	3. Open an issue [here](https://github.com/HexRaysSA/plugin-repository/issues) and Hex-Rays will be happy to help debug
271	
272	
273	The indexer runs daily, so it might take a little time for your plugin to show up.
274	Feel free to ping us and we can manually trigger a rebuild to check for your new plugin.
275	
276	
277	### How can I report a suspicious/malicious plugin?
278	
279	Open an issue on the plugin repository and the Hex-Rays team will investigate and potentially update the index.
280	
281	
282	### How does moderation work?
283	
284	Plugins can be removed from the plugin repository so that HCLI does not serve them to users.
285	
286	At a technical level, the plugin repository *is* the JSON file available [here](https://github.com/HexRaysSA/plugin-repository).
287	Its produced by an indexer that runs periodically, and uses a [denylist](https://github.com/HexRaysSA/plugin-repository/blob/v1/ignored-repositories.txt) to filter out repositories that Hex-Rays deems inappropriate (malware, illegal, abusive, etc.).
288	Because the entire repository is within a git repository on GitHub, anyone can review the enforcement actions (such as adding to the denylist) and see what has happened.
289	We designed transparency into the system from the start, to help everyone understand and trust the infrastructure.
290	
291	### I previously submitted my plugin via My Hex-Rays portal. What should I do now?
292	
293	Follow the guidelines on [making your plugin compatible with Plugin Manager](../reference/packaging-your-existing-plugin.md). Once completed, your plugin will be included in the central index and available directly through the Plugin Manager.
294	
295	If your plugin is hosted in the same repository used for your previous submission to [plugins.hex-rays.com](https://plugins.hex-rays.com/), and the repository URL remains unchanged, we’ll automatically update its details on the website.

1	## Plugin Packaging and Format
2	
3	A Plugin Archive is a ZIP archive that contains an IDA plugin and its associated `ida-plugin.json` metadata file.
4	The metadata file should be found in the root directory of the plugin within the archive.
5	
6	For example:
7	
8	```
9	plugin.zip
10	├── ida-plugin.json
11	└── plugin.py
12	```
13	
14	Or for a native plugin:
15	
16	```
17	plugin.zip
18	├── ida-plugin.json
19	├── plugin.so
20	├── plugin.dylib
21	└── plugin.dll
22	```
23	
24	### ida-plugin.json
25	
26	The [`ida-plugin.json` file](https://docs.hex-rays.com/developer/publishing-plugins/how-tos/plugin-publishing) is the marker for an IDA Pro plugin.
27	A typical `ida-plugin.json` file might look like this:
28	
29	```json
30	{
31	  "$schema": "https://hcli.docs.hex-rays.com/schemas/ida-plugin.json",
32	  "IDAMetadataDescriptorVersion": 1,
33	  "plugin": {
34	    "name": "oplog",
35	    "entryPoint": "oplog_entry.py",
36	    "version": "0.1.2",
37	    "idaVersions": ["9.1", "9.2"],
38	    "description": "oplog is an IDA Pro plugin that records operations during analysis.",
39	    "license": "Apache 2.0",
40	    "categories": [
41	      "ui-ux-and-visualization"
42	    ],
43	    "pythonDependencies": ["pydantic>=2"],
44	    "urls": {
45	      "repository": "https://github.com/williballenthin/idawilli"
46	    },
47	    "authors": [{
48	      "name": "Willi Ballenthin",
49	      "email": "wballenthin@hex-rays.com"
50	    }],
51	    "keywords": [
52	      "activity-tracking",
53	      "workflow-analysis",
54	      "reverse-engineering-methodology",
55	      "ai-training-data",
56	      "analysis-visualization"
57	    ]
58	  }
59	}
60	```
61	
62	And a minimal `ida-plugin.json` could look like this:
63	
64	```json
65	{
66	  "$schema": "https://hcli.docs.hex-rays.com/schemas/ida-plugin.json",
67	  "IDAMetadataDescriptorVersion": 1,
68	  "plugin": {
69	    "name": "oplog",
70	    "entryPoint": "oplog_entry.py",
71	    "version": "0.1.2",
72	    "urls": {
73	      "repository": "https://github.com/williballenthin/idawilli"
74	    },
75	    "authors": [{
76	      "name": "Willi Ballenthin",
77	      "email": "wballenthin@hex-rays.com"
78	    }]
79	  }
80	}
81	```
82	
83	In addition to the primary fields described initially on the [Hex-Rays docs](https://docs.hex-rays.com/developer/publishing-plugins/how-tos/plugin-publishing), **HCLI compatibility added new, required fields** in `ida-plugin.json`:
84	
85	  - `version`: the version of the plugin archive
86	  - `urls.repository`: the repository that publishes the plugin
87	  - `authors` (or `maintainers`): name and/or email. Social media handles are ok!
88	
89	And there are new optional fields:
90	
91	  - `.plugin.pythonDependencies` is a list of packages on PyPI that will be installed
92	  - `.plugin.keywords` is a list of terms to help users searching for plugins
93	  - `.plugin.platforms` is recommended, defaults to all platforms. The possible values are: `windows-x86_64`, `linux-x86_64`, `macos-x86_64`, and `macos-aarch64`.
94	  - `.plugin.license` for the code license of your project
95	  - `.plugin.settings` is a list of descriptors of settings
96	
97	If there's a problem with the `ida-plugin.json` file, then the plugin is invalid and won't work with the repo.
98	Unfortunately even things like trailing commas will break strict JSON parsers like the one used by HCLI.
99	So, you can use `hcli plugin lint /path/to/plugin[.zip]` to check for problems and suggestions.
100	
101	!!! tip "Editor validation with JSON Schema"
102	
103	    HCLI publishes a JSON Schema for `ida-plugin.json` at
104	    [`https://hcli.docs.hex-rays.com/schemas/ida-plugin.json`](https://hcli.docs.hex-rays.com/schemas/ida-plugin.json).
105	
106	    Reference it from the top of your `ida-plugin.json` to get inline validation,
107	    autocompletion, and hover documentation in editors like VSCode:
108	
109	    ```json
110	    {
111	      "$schema": "https://hcli.docs.hex-rays.com/schemas/ida-plugin.json",
112	      "IDAMetadataDescriptorVersion": 1,
113	      "plugin": { ... }
114	    }
115	    ```
116	
117	    The schema is generated from the same Pydantic models HCLI uses to validate

121	### Shared Settings
122	
123	HCLI is aware of settings that plugins declare in `ida-plugin.json` and prompts users for their value
124	during installation. The settings are written into `ida-config.json` and can be queried at plugin runtime
125	using the [ida-settings](https://pypi.org/project/ida-settings/) (v3) Python package:
126	
127	```py
128	import ida_settings
129	
130	api_key = ida_settings.get_current_plugin_setting("openai_key")
131	```
132	
133	Plugin authors are encouraged to adopt this configuration system, as it provides a centralized way to manage edits from both the CLI and (eventually) the GUI, users don't have to manually edit source code/config files,
134	and the data can be easily exported/imported.
135	
136	!!! note "Coming Soon"
137	
138	      The associated IDA plugin `ida-settings-editor` that lets users configure plugin settings within IDA is not yet available. We plan to introduce it in a future release.
139	
140	#### Setting Fields
141	
142	Each setting in the `settings` array supports the following fields:
143	
144	| Field | Type | Required | Description |
145	|-------|------|----------|-------------|
146	| `key` | string | yes | Unique code-level identifier (e.g., `"api_key"`) |
147	| `type` | string | yes | Either `"string"` or `"boolean"` |
148	| `required` | boolean | yes | Whether the setting must be provided |
149	| `default` | string/boolean | no | Default value when not configured |
150	| `name` | string | yes | Human-readable name (e.g., `"OpenAI API key"`) |
151	| `documentation` | string | no | Human-readable explanation |
152	| `validation_pattern` | string | no | Regex pattern for string validation |
153	| `choices` | array | no | List of acceptable string values |
154	| `prompt` | boolean | no | Whether to prompt during installation (default: `true`) |
155	
156	Setting `"prompt": false` is useful for advanced or niche settings that have sensible defaults and shouldn't clutter the installation experience. These settings can still be configured later via `hcli plugin config`.
157	
158	Example settings configuration:
159	
160	```json
161	{
162	  "settings": [
163	    {
164	      "key": "api_key",
165	      "type": "string",
166	      "required": true,
167	      "name": "API Key",
168	      "documentation": "Your API key from https://example.com/keys"
169	    },
170	    {
171	      "key": "cache_size",
172	      "type": "string",
173	      "required": false,
174	      "default": "100",
175	      "name": "Cache Size",
176	      "documentation": "Maximum number of cached items",
177	      "prompt": false
178	    }
179	  ]
180	}
181	```

184	### Source Archives and Binary Archives
185	
186	For many pure-Python IDA plugins, source archives are often sufficient.
187	This means you don't have to create any GitHub Actions workflows; you just have to tag your releases in GitHub.
188	
189	If you distribute your pure-Python IDA plugin via PyPI, [like IPyIDA does](https://github.com/eset/ipyida),
190	then the plugin directory in your source archive becomes very simple.
191	You can put the following content in a subdirectory of the project (preferred), or publish a separate repository for the metadata:
192	
193	
194	```
195	.
196	├── ida-plugin.json
197	└── entry_stub.py
198	```
199	
200	With `ida-plugin.json`:
201	
202	```json
203	{
204	  "$schema": "https://hcli.docs.hex-rays.com/schemas/ida-plugin.json",
205	  "IDAMetadataDescriptorVersion": 1,
206	  "plugin": {
207	    "name": "plugin1",
208	    "entryPoint": "entry_stub.py",
209	    "version": "1.0",
210	    "idaVersions": ["9.0", "9.1", "9.2"],
211	    "pythonDependencies": ["ida-plugin1==1.0"],
212	    "urls": {
213	      "repository": "https://github.com/foo/bar"
214	    },
215	    "authors": [{
216	      "email": "user@example.com"
217	    }]
218	  }
219	}
220	```
221	
222	And the entry stub:
223	
224	
225	```py
226	from ida_plugin1.ida_plugin import PLUGIN_ENTRY
227	```

229	### "Fat" Binary Plugin Archives
230	
231	Plugin archives can contain multiple compiled versions of a plugin, e.g., `foo-plugin.so` and `foo-plugin.dylib`.
232	In this case, the entry point must specify the bare path to the plugin, e.g., `foo-plugin`, and IDA will append the appropriate extension based on the platform.
233	You don't have to support all platforms. It's acceptable to publish multiple "thin" archives, one for each platform; however, "fat" archives are convenient.
234	
235	The file extensions must be exactly:
236	
237	  - `.dll` - Windows x86-64
238	  - `.so` - Linux 86-64
239	  - `_x86_64.dylib` - macOS x86_64 (not yet supported by IDA)
240	  - `_aarch64.dylib` - macOS aarch64 (not yet supported by IDA)
241	  - `.dylib` - macOS Universal Binary, only if Intel/ARM dylibs aren't present. (note: you must use this for macOS currently)
242	
243	
244	
245	Remember, plugin names must be unique within a plugin archive, which means:
246	
247	Allowed:
248	```
249	root/
250	  plugin/
251	    ida-plugin.json (name: foo-plugin)
252	    foo-plugin.so
253	    foo-plugin.dylib
254	    foo-plugin.dll
255	```
256	
257	Disallowed:
258	```
259	root/

1	# CI/CD Integration
2	
3	## Overview
4	
5	HCLI is designed to work in automated environments like CI/CD pipelines. This guide shows you how to:
6	
7	- Authenticate HCLI in automated environments
8	- Install IDA Pro in CI/CD runners
9	- Download IDA SDKs for building plugins
10	- Test IDA Pro plugins automatically
11	
12	Using HCLI in CI/CD enables you to:
13	
14	- **Automate plugin builds** across multiple IDA versions
15	- **Test plugins** against different IDA releases
16	- **Build native plugins** using the IDA SDK
17	- **Verify plugin compatibility** before releasing
18	- **Deploy plugins** to the Hex-Rays plugin repository
19	
20	## Authentication for CI/CD
21	
22	### Using API Keys
23	
24	API keys are the recommended authentication method for automated environments. Unlike OAuth, API keys don't require browser interaction and can be securely stored as CI/CD secrets.
25	
26	### Creating an API Key
27	
28	First, create an API key for your CI/CD system:
29	
30	```bash
31	hcli auth key create --name "my-project-ci"
32	The key will be displayed only once, so make sure to save it in a secure place.
33	? Do you want to create a new API key my-project-ci? (Y/n) Yes
34	API key created: REDACTED
35	```
36	
37	**Important:** Save this key immediately - it won't be shown again!
38	
39	### Setting the Environment Variable
40	
41	HCLI automatically uses the `HCLI_API_KEY` environment variable for authentication:
42	
43	```bash
44	export REDACTED
45	```
46	
47	When this environment variable is set, HCLI will use it for all API requests without requiring interactive login.
48	
49	Verify authentication:
50	
51	```bash
52	hcli whoami
53	You are logged in as user@example.com using an API key from HCLI_API_KEY environment variable
54	```
55	
56	### Security Best Practices
57	
58	1. **Never commit API keys to version control** - Always use CI/CD secret management
59	2. **Use descriptive key names** - Include the project and purpose (e.g., "zydis-github-actions")
60	3. **Create separate keys per project** - This allows independent key rotation and revocation
61	4. **Rotate keys periodically** - Revoke old keys and create new ones regularly
62	5. **Monitor key usage** - Use `hcli auth key list` to check when keys were last used
63	6. **Revoke unused keys** - Clean up keys that are no longer needed
64	
65	For more details, see [Authentication](../getting-started/authentication.md) and [Environment Variables](../reference/environment-variables.md).

68	
69	### Installing IDA Pro
70	
71	This example shows how to install IDA Pro in a GitHub Actions workflow for developing plugins that require a full IDA installation:
72	
73	```yaml
74	name: Test Plugin
75	
76	on:
77	  push:
78	    branches: [ main ]
79	  pull_request:
80	    branches: [ main ]
81	
82	jobs:
83	  test:
84	    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
85	
86	    steps:
87	      - name: Checkout code
88	        uses: actions/checkout@v4
89	
90	      - name: Set up Python
91	        uses: actions/setup-python@v5
92	        with:
93	          python-version: '3.11'
94	
95	      - name: Install HCLI
96	        run: |
97	          pip install ida-hcli
98	
99	      - name: Authenticate HCLI
100	        env:
101	          HCLI_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.HCLI_API_KEY }}
102	        run: |
103	          hcli whoami
104	
105	      - name: Install IDA Pro
106	        env:
107	          HCLI_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.HCLI_API_KEY }}
108	        run: |
109	          hcli ida install \
110	            --yes \
111	            --accept-eula \
112	            --set-default \
113	            --create-python-environment \
114	            --license-id ${{ secrets.IDA_LICENSE_ID }} \
115	            --download-id release/9.2/ida-pro/ida-pro_92_x64linux.run

1	# IDA Plugin Repository Architecture
2	
3	## Core Components
4	
5	1. **User-facing portal showcasing the plugins** - The [plugins.hex-rays.com](https://plugins.hex-rays.com/) is a web interface to the collection of available IDA Pro plugins.
6	2. **JSON Index** - The new plugin repository publishes a JSON document within [github.com/HexRaysSA/plugin-repository](https://github.com/HexRaysSA/plugin-repository). This file is the index of all available plugins, their versions and metadata, and download URLs.
7	3. **GitHub Actions** - GitHub Actions runs regularly to update the JSON document with plugins discovered across GitHub. The raw index data is available [here](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HexRaysSA/plugin-repository/refs/heads/v1/plugin-repository.json).
8	4. **Named repositories** - hcli reads its repositories from `.Settings.plugin-repositories` in `ida-config.json` and merges them client-side, so it always knows which repository served a plugin. Two are shipped and reserved: `community` (`https://community.plugins.hex-rays.com/plugin-repository.json`, anonymous) and `hexrays` (`https://hexrays.plugins.hex-rays.com/plugin-repository.json`, which requires `hcli login` and serves only the private plugins your account is entitled to). Manage the rest with `hcli plugin repo list | add | remove | set-default`.
9	
10	    A reference may name a repository: `hcli plugin install hexrays/<name>`. Without a prefix it resolves in the repository named by `.Settings.default-plugin-repository` (`community` by default), while `hcli plugin search` spans every configured repository and reports any it could not reach.
11	
12	
13	## How It Works
14	
15	The plugin repository's GitHub Action watches for GitHub repositories that contain an `ida-plugin.json` file.
16	For each repo, it will watch for releases. When it sees a release, it will inspect the release archives for either source archives (pure-Python) or binary archives (containing .so/.dll/.dylib plugins).
17	In either case, it'll expect to find an `ida-plugin.json` file in the archive describing the plugin.
18	The service will index all the found archives and their metadata, and expose this to HCLI
19	(and/or other plugin managers, like a planned GUI version within IDA).
20	
21	!!! note
22	
23	    The plugin repository requires additional metadata compared to the initial version documented on the Hex-Rays docs website.
24	
25	
26	## IDA Plugin Manager
27	
28	HCLI uses the plugin repository JSON file to list/search for plugins and retrieve the download URL.
29	After various validation steps, HCLI then extracts the archive subdirectory containing
30	 `ida-plugin.json` into `$IDAUSR/plugins/`, and the plugin is installed.
31	If there are Python dependencies declared within the metadata file, then these are installed via pip first.
32	There are obvious upgrade and uninstallation routines, too.
33	
34	### Plugin Installation Location
35	
36	Plugins are installed to `$IDAUSR/plugins/`, where `$IDAUSR` is the IDA user directory: 
37	
38	- **Windows**: `%APPDATA%\Hex-Rays\IDA Pro\`
39	- **macOS**: `~/Library/Application Support/IDA Pro/`
40	- **Linux**: `~/.idapro/`
41	
42	It's possible to override `$IDAUSR` when running IDA, which can be helpful if you test across multiple versions:
43	
44	```
45	$ export IDAUSR=~/.idapro91/
46	$ hcli plugin install ipyida
47	$ ~/software/ida-9.1/ida
48	```
49	
50	Each plugin is installed in its own subdirectory within `plugins/`. For example, installing the "oplog" plugin creates:
51	```
52	$IDAUSR/plugins/oplog/
53	├── ida-plugin.json
54	├── oplog_entry.py
55	└── (other plugin files)
56	```
57	
58	The directory name matches the plugin name from `ida-plugin.json`.
59	This is why the contents of `name` are fairly restrictive. They should also be globally unique.
60	
61	During upgrades, the existing directory is replaced with the new version.
62	Uninstallation is as easy as deleting the directory.
63	
64	### Plugin identity and name collisions
65	
66	In the repository index, a plugin is identified by the pair `(name, repository URL)`. Two plugins with the same bare name from different repositories are distinct entries, and the repository URL is normalized (lowercased scheme/host/path, trailing slash stripped) before comparison so that cosmetic URL differences do not split a single plugin into two.
67	
68	On disk, however, plugins still install as `$IDAUSR/plugins/<name>`. Name is therefore the installed-layout identity, and only one plugin with a given bare name can be installed at a time. When the repository contains multiple plugins with the same name, HCLI requires a qualified reference of the form `name@repository-url` (optionally with a version spec, e.g. `name==1.2.3@repository-url`). An installed plugin's local metadata records its source repository, so status and upgrade operations anchor their repository lookups on the installed plugin's host and stay consistent even when the bare name is ambiguous in the repository.

1	# HCLI plugin bundle specification
2	
3	## Goal
4	
5	HCLI must be able to install IDA plugins and their Python dependencies on machines that cannot reach the network. A connected machine builds a plugin bundle archive. An offline machine can copy that archive locally and use normal plugin manager commands against it.
6	
7	The plugin bundle is repository-level. It may contain multiple plugins, multiple versions, and the shared wheelhouses (directories of pre-downloaded `.whl` files) needed to install those plugins. It is not a per-plugin sandbox, and it does not change HCLI's current dependency installation model: Python dependencies are installed into the active IDA Python environment.
8	
9	## Supported user flows
10	
11	Create a plugin bundle on a connected machine targeting the current machine's platform and Python:
12	
13	```console
14	hcli plugin bundle create \
15	  --path malware-vm-tools-2026-04.hcli-plugin-bundle.zip \
16	  --platform current --python current \
17	  oplog==0.1.3 \
18	  hint-calls==0.1.3
19	```
20	
21	Both `--platform` and `--python` are always required. The special value `current` resolves to the current machine's platform or Python version. The special value `all` resolves to all supported platforms (linux, windows, macos-arm64, macos-intel) or all supported Python versions (3.10–3.14). Otherwise, pass a specific name like `linux` or version like `3.12`.
22

92	## Command-line interface

98	```
99	
100	`--repo` accepts the existing repository forms plus a local plugin bundle archive. A plugin bundle archive is a ZIP file containing top-level `plugin-bundle.json`.
101	
102	`--pip-index-url` is passed to pip as `--index-url`. It may point to PyPI, Artifactory, or any other compatible package index.
103	
104	`--pip-extra-index-url` is repeatable and passed to pip as `--extra-index-url`.
105	
106	`--pip-find-links` is repeatable and passed to pip as `--find-links`.
107	
108	`--offline` forces pip dependency resolution to use only local sources. It passes `--no-index` and must be used with either a plugin bundle wheelhouse or at least one `--pip-find-links` value.
109	
110	Pip source precedence is:
111	
112	1. Explicit pip CLI options.
113	2. Plugin bundle wheelhouse selected from the active plugin bundle.
114	3. Existing configured/default online pip behavior.
115	
116	If explicit pip CLI options are provided while using a plugin bundle repository, the explicit options control dependency installation. The plugin bundle still controls plugin discovery and plugin archive bytes.
117	
118	## Plugin bundle archive format
119	
120	A plugin bundle archive is a ZIP file with this layout:
121	
122	```text
123	plugin-bundle.json
124	plugins/
125	  <archive-name>.zip
126	dependencies/
127	  python/
128	    <target-id>/
129	      <wheel files>.whl
130	```
131	
132	The `plugins/` directory contains unmodified IDA plugin ZIP archives. HCLI discovers bundled plugins by walking `plugins/` and reading `ida-plugin.json` from each archive.
133	
134	Each `dependencies/python/<target-id>/` directory is a flat wheelhouse for one target tuple. Wheels keep their original filenames. Sdists are rejected by default during bundle creation.
135	
136	Each target entry in the manifest is a snapshot of the exact compatibility parameters used to fetch wheels for that target. This allows audit and install to verify wheel compatibility without re-deriving the parameters.
137	
138	`plugin-bundle.json` is UTF-8 JSON. Version 1 has this shape:
139	
140	```json
141	{
142	  "version": 1,
143	  "kind": "hcli-plugin-bundle",
144	  "builtAt": "2026-04-28T16:00:00Z",
145	  "createdBy": {
146	    "tool": "hcli",
147	    "version": "0.0.0"
148	  },
149	  "targetPlatformTags": [
150	    {
151	      "id": "linux-x86_64-cp312",
152	      "idaPlatform": "linux-x86_64",
153	      "pythonVersion": "3.12",
154	      "implementation": "cp",
155	      "abis": ["cp312", "abi3", "none"],
156	      "pipPlatformTags": [
157	        "manylinux_2_28_x86_64",
158	        "manylinux_2_17_x86_64",
159	        "manylinux2014_x86_64"
160	      ],
161	      "wheelhouse": "dependencies/python/linux-x86_64-cp312"
162	    }
163	  ]
164	}
165	```

167	## Target matching
168	
169	On install or upgrade, HCLI detects the active IDA platform and active IDA Python interpreter. For IDA 9.0+, the first supported Python line is Python 3.10+.
170	
171	HCLI selects a wheelhouse whose target tuple matches:
172	
173	- HCLI/IDA platform, such as `windows-x86_64` or `macos-aarch64`
174	- Python major/minor version
175	- CPython implementation and ABI expectations
176	
177	If no target tuple matches, HCLI fails before changing plugins or installing dependencies.
178	
179	A plugin bundle may contain target tuples for operating systems and Python versions other than the machine that created it. Cross-target creation is supported when every dependency can be obtained as a compatible wheel for the requested target. If a required dependency is available only as an sdist, or only as a wheel with a platform baseline newer than the target, bundle creation or audit must fail for that target unless the user supplies a matching prebuilt wheel.
180	
181	### IDA version compatibility during bundle creation
182	
183	Bundle creation does not check IDA version compatibility. The builder machine may run a different IDA version than the target machines, and plugin `idaVersions` metadata is not a useful filtering axis during packaging. Plugins are bundled as-is; IDA version compatibility is checked only at install time on the target machine. This avoids adding IDA version as yet another dimension to the target matrix (alongside platform and Python version) and keeps the bundle creation model simple. If users report problems with this approach, IDA version filtering can be revisited.
184	
185	## Dependency installation behavior
186	
187	When installing a plugin with `pythonDependencies`, HCLI installs dependencies with pip before extracting the plugin. When a plugin bundle is in use, HCLI extracts the matching wheelhouse to a temporary directory and adds it as a `--find-links` source. By default pip can still reach online indexes, so a bundle with an incomplete wheelhouse will fall back to downloading missing wheels. When the user passes `--offline`, HCLI adds `--no-index` so pip resolves only from local sources:
188	
189	```console
190	python -m pip install \
191	  --isolated \
192	  --disable-pip-version-check \
193	  --no-cache-dir \
194	  [--no-index]           # only when --offline is passed \
195	  --find-links <temporary-wheelhouse> \
196	  <all dependency specs>
197	```
198	
199	HCLI includes dependency specs from already installed HCLI-managed plugins plus the plugin being installed or upgraded. Already installed packages may satisfy requirements if pip considers them compatible. HCLI does not use `--ignore-installed` by default.
200	
201	No hash pinning is required. The user trusts the plugin bundle author.
202	
203	HCLI does not uninstall Python dependencies when plugins are uninstalled. Orphaned dependencies are left in the Python environment, matching current behavior.
204	
205	## Bundle creation behavior
206	
207	`hcli plugin bundle create` accepts explicit plugin versions and local plugin ZIP paths as positional arguments. Repository plugin references must include an exact version, for example `oplog==0.1.3`. Bare latest resolution is intentionally not part of the first version. `--path` selects the output archive path.
208	
209	Targeting uses `--platform` and `--python`, both required and repeatable. Each accepts `current` (auto-detect this machine), `all` (all supported values), or a specific value. `--platform` accepts the canonical IDA platform name (e.g. `linux-x86_64`) or short aliases (`linux`, `windows`, `macos-arm64`, `macos-intel`). `--python` accepts a `major.minor` version string (e.g. `3.12`). HCLI builds the cross product of all resolved platforms and Python versions. Duplicate targets are deduplicated.
210	
211	The supported Python versions for `--python all` are maintained as a hardcoded constant (`SUPPORTED_PYTHON_VERSIONS`): 3.10, 3.11, 3.12, 3.13, 3.14. This is updated when new Python versions release (annually in October). This matches the approach used by cibuildwheel and other ecosystem tools — no package provides this list dynamically.
212	
213	A legacy `--target` flag (e.g. `--target linux-x86_64-cp312`) is accepted for scripting but hidden from help. It cannot be combined with `--platform` or `--python`.
214	
215	Bundle creation resolves all selected plugin archives, reads their `ida-plugin.json` metadata, collects all `pythonDependencies`, and materializes a flat wheelhouse per target tuple. A single online Linux builder can create wheelhouses for all target platforms when all dependencies publish compatible wheels.
216	
217	The preferred wheelhouse materialization path is one `pip download` invocation per target. For cross-target downloads HCLI must pass all compatibility options together:
218	
219	```console
220	python -m pip download \
221	  --only-binary=:all: \
222	  --implementation cp \
223	  --python-version <major.minor> \
224	  --abi <cp-abi> --abi abi3 --abi none \
225	  --platform <platform-tag> [--platform <platform-tag> ...] \
226	  --dest <wheelhouse> \
227	  -r <requirements-or-lock>
228	```
229	
230	`--platform` is repeatable. Linux targets should list every manylinux tag HCLI accepts, for example `manylinux_2_28_x86_64`, `manylinux_2_17_x86_64`, and `manylinux2014_x86_64`. macOS x86_64 targets should include the supported deployment baseline. Optional targets such as Windows ARM64 or musllinux should be explicit presets rather than inferred from x86_64 targets. Over-listing compatible tags is safer than under-listing them.
231	
232	`uv pip compile --universal` may be used to produce one cross-platform lock or constraints file before materializing target wheelhouses. `uv pip install --python-platform ... --python ... --target ...` is also valid for producing an unpacked per-target site-packages tree; because the version 1 plugin bundle format stores wheel files, `pip download` remains the direct path for wheelhouse plugin bundles unless HCLI later adds an unpacked dependency tree format.
233	
234	By default, bundle creation rejects sdists because offline installation from sdists requires build tools and build dependencies on the target. Missing wheels are handled by failing the affected target, by using a matching builder to produce wheels, or by supplying prebuilt wheels with a local `--find-links` source. Linux wheels can often be built from one Linux host inside a manylinux container. Windows and macOS sdist-only dependencies require native runners or prebuilt vendor wheels.
235	
236	If selected plugins have incompatible Python dependency constraints, bundle creation fails.
237	
238	## Additive plugin bundles
239	
240	Plugin bundles are additive. An offline VM may use one plugin bundle today and a second plugin bundle later. HCLI does not require a single authoritative plugin bundle for the machine.
241	
242	When a plugin bundle install fails, errors should distinguish where possible: whether the plugin is absent from the bundle, whether it exists but is incompatible with the current IDA version or platform, whether no wheelhouse matches the active IDA Python, whether a dependency wheel is missing from the selected wheelhouse, or whether dependency constraints conflict with already installed packages.
243	
244	## Private plugin metadata
245	
246	The `repository` field in `ida-plugin.json` must be a valid GitHub URL (`https://github.com/org/project`). This applies to both public and private plugins. Private plugins should use a GitHub repository URL — either a public repo or a private one. If no real repository exists, a placeholder GitHub URL is acceptable (e.g. `https://github.com/internal/placeholder`) because the public plugin indexer only fetches URLs for plugins it ingests, and offline bundle plugins are never indexed.
247	
248	The validation is intentionally not relaxed to support arbitrary hosting providers (GitLab, Gitea, etc.) until there are concrete user requirements. Keeping the GitHub constraint preserves the field's usefulness as a consistent, predictable link format across all plugins.
249	
250	## Plugin spec disambiguation
251	
252	When the plugin repository contains multiple entries with the same plugin name from different hosts (e.g. forks), `bundle create` requires the `@host` suffix to disambiguate:
253	
254	```console
255	hcli plugin bundle create \
256	  --path bundle.zip \
257	  --platform all --python all \
258	  "efiXplorer==6.2.0@https://github.com/rehints/efixplorer" \
259	  "idalib-rust-bindings==0.9.0@https://github.com/idalib-rs/idalib"
260	```

262	The `@host` is parsed from the spec before resolution. Unambiguous plugins do not require it.

264	## Known limitations observed during all-plugin bundle testing
265	
266	Bundle creation pools all `pythonDependencies` from every included plugin into a single `pip download` invocation per target. A single unresolvable dependency (nonexistent version, missing wheel for the target) fails the entire wheelhouse for that target. There is no per-plugin isolation.
